title: ML inference budget workshop - Kaleida Systems
summary: Discovery-style workshop focused on per-token unit economics, batching/caching levers, and tradeoffs across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Customer has strong latency constraints for realtime features but is budget sensitive; exploring hybrid hosting + dedicated fallbacks. Agreed next steps include a tailored unit-econ spreadsheet, security docs, and a small pilot for a 2-week latency benchmark.
action_items: Maya Chen - Send tailored unit-econ spreadsheet and example token assumptions - due 2027-04-05
Liam O'Connor - Provide recommended batching and quantization profile for their 2k token seqs (rough estimate) - due 2027-04-06
Priya Rao - Share current request distribution (p95 latency target / token histogram) with Redwood - due 2027-04-04
Maya Chen - Share SOC2 and security questionnaire; schedule Private deployment technical follow-up if they pass initial review - due 2027-04-07
next_steps: Redwood to send unit economics model and baseline hosted pricing
Customer to provide traffic histograms and example prompts
Schedule 2-week pilot to run latency benchmarks (hosted then dedicated fallback)
Security docs and KMS integration review
transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-04-02 14:30 UTC | Duration: ~55m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Kaleida CTO), Marcus Hale (Head of ML), Anya Sato (Infra), Diego Ramos (Product)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. do you want to do quick intros and then we can jump into budget and unit econ?
[00:15] Priya Rao: Yeah, thanks Maya. I'm Priya, CTO at Kaleida. we've been prototyping a realtime assistant in our app, so latency's a big deal. Marcus and Anya are here to dig into infra and cost.
[00:28] Marcus Hale: hi all. our target is sub 250ms for p95 on the short-form prompts, 2k tokens is worst-case but most calls are under 600 tokens. cost is... we have runway limits so we need to show a path to <$0.0008 per user request ideally.
[00:45] Liam O'Connor: okay, useful. at a high level Redwood offers Hosted for fastest start, Dedicated reserved pools for predictable throughput, and Private for on-prem/VPC with more compliance. each has tradeoffs on unit cost and latency.
[00:58] Anya Sato: can you remind us quickly what changes unit cost most? is it model choice, batching, or the infra?
[01:12] Liam O'Connor: all three. model size and quantization changes per-token compute; batching and request coalescing improve GPU utilization; KV/prefix cache means repeated prefixes cost near-zero after warmup. sequence length matters a lot: doubling tokens roughly doubles compute.
[01:28] Diego Ramos: when you say batch, are users okay with higher tail latencies? our UX team worries.
[01:35] Maya Chen: good point. Redwood's continuous batching tries to optimize without adding much tail, and we have routing policies -- for strict SLO calls you can route to a low-latency pool or use an autoscale reserve. but that increases cost.
[01:50] Marcus Hale: can you quantify? like hosted baseline for a 70B open model vs dedicated?
[02:00] Liam O'Connor: rough ballpark: hosted per-token price factors include managed overhead and multi-tenant margins so could be 15-30% higher than a well-utilized dedicated pool. dedicated amortizes GPU cost but you need commit/capacity planning. for small volume, hosted often wins economically. for steady high volume, dedicated plus batching + int8/q4 quantization can be cheaper per token by 30-50%.
[02:28] Priya Rao: our volume is spiky, think 7x daily peak. can Redwood handle burst without overprovisioning?
[02:37] Maya Chen: yes—burst capacity and autoscale policies. you can provision a baseline dedicated pool and fallback to hosted for bursts; that's a common hybrid pattern. fallback routing does add egress and possible model variant mismatch so you should test for quality drift.
[02:52] Anya Sato: security—our compliance team requires SOC2 and KMS for keys, also we need audit logs retention for a year. does Redwood Private make this easier?
[03:03] Rav Patel: Redwood Private offers customer-controlled KMS, audit logs, and can be deployed in their VPC or on-prem. Hosted can meet SOC2 but KMS integration and long-term log retention are enterprise add-ons.
[03:18] Marcus Hale: good. let's talk specifics: our average prompt is 420 tokens, average response 180 tokens, so ~600 tokens per request. target p95 250ms. budget target per request <$0.0008. what are levers we should consider?
[03:34] Liam O'Connor: levers: 1) model family and size (smaller model = fewer tokens cost but possible quality drop), 2) quantization (int8/q4) reduces compute, 3) batching behavior and max wait window, 4) prefix/KV cache for repetitive contexts, 5) routing hybrid (hosted fallback during peaks). we'll run numbers against your 600-token baseline.
[03:55] Diego Ramos: can you do a quick hypothetical calc?
[04:00] Liam O'Connor: okay rough: assume a 33B model with q4 gives you baseline compute X. hosted rate might be $0.0014 per 1k tokens (example), so for 600 tokens that's $0.00084—just above your target. with dedicated and steady batching, that could drop to $0.0005 per request. with aggressive KV caching on commonly repeated system prompts maybe further to $0.0003. these are illustrative; we'll model with your traffic.
[04:29] Priya Rao: those hosted numbers seem close—what hidden costs should we plan for?
[04:34] Maya Chen: network egress, storage (KV cache), and burst pricing for dedicated fallback. also engineering effort to integrate SDKs and manage model rollouts. Redwood Console's cost breakdown helps make those explicit.
[04:48] Marcus Hale: our prompts are highly template-driven, lots of repeated prefix content. how easy is it to use KV caching?
[04:56] Liam O'Connor: pretty straightforward. server-side prefix cache can be sticky per user session; when your app reuses same system prompt the token delta is small. we usually see 20-40% token savings on assistant-style workflows.
[05:10] Anya Sato: ok, timeline—if we pilot, what's the smallest scope to prove economics?
[05:17] Maya Chen: two-week pilot: run a representative subset of traffic against hosted baseline, enable Redwood Dedicated fallback to simulate peaks, measure p95 and unit cost. include a set of control prompts to monitor quality drift.
[05:31] Diego Ramos: what sample size do you need?
[05:34] Liam O'Connor: a few hundred thousand tokens a day across the two weeks gives good signal. if you don't have that in prod we can synthesize traffic with similar token distribution.
[05:45] Priya Rao: we can probably carve out our beta cohort for that.
[05:49] Marcus Hale: quick question: quantization impact on latency—does q4 give us much latency improvement?
[05:55] Liam O'Connor: quantization reduces memory and sometimes ops cost; on GPUs you also get kernel-level speedups. Q4 often reduces latency modestly and reduces memory pressure, enabling larger batch sizes at same GPU. but quality tradeoffs vary by model.
[06:10] Priya Rao: we care about hallucination risk too. can you run evals to show quality delta?
[06:15] Maya Chen: yes, Redwood Optimize can run prompt set evals and surface regressions tied to a model/config change. we'll include that in the pilot scope.
[06:25] Anya Sato: how do we think about fallback routing and model variants? if dedicated doesn't have the same quantization or variant, do you degrade?
[06:34] Ravi Patel: routing policies allow fallbacks to compatible variants; we recommend version pinning and a quality guardrail in the console for automatic rollback if regression detected. there is some risk of small behavior differences when using quantized variants as fallback—part of pilot is to test quality across routes.
[06:51] Diego Ramos: what's the typical SLA for dedicated latency?
[06:55] Liam O'Connor: SLA targets depend on the committed pool and model. we publish latency profiles per model; with dedicated reserved capacity you can target low-100ms p95 for short sequences on optimized kernels. longer sequences increase p95.
[07:12] Priya Rao: Let's talk budget math. Marcus: what's our monthly token budget allowance?
[07:17] Marcus Hale: initial budget is $35k/month for inference.
[07:21] Maya Chen: with $35k you can achieve a lot. we'll build a run-rate model showing hosted only vs hybrid vs dedicated with commit options.
[07:29] Marcus Hale: can you show break-even point for dedicated?
[07:33] Liam O'Connor: yes, typically break-even depends on utilization; often in our data it occurs around sustained tens of millions of tokens per month for mid-sized models, but with good batching and caching you can reduce the threshold. we'll run scenarios against your 600-token avg and spike patterns.
[07:50] Priya Rao: compliance again—if we need HSM-level KMS and a separate key store, is that doable?
[07:57] Ravi Patel: yes, Private supports HSM/KMS integration and customer-controlled keys. for Hosted, we offer KMS integrations with caveats; we'll share the security datasheet.
[08:09] Anya Sato: what's the onboarding friction for Private?
[08:12] Maya Chen: Private is more involved—networking, firewall rules, and possibly on-prem ops. typical lead time is a few weeks to months depending on infra, but many customers start with Hosted then move to Private.
[08:24] Diego Ramos: ok, what are the immediate risks we should watch?
[08:27] Liam O'Connor: 1) QA drift with quantized/fallback models, 2) underestimating peak capacity, 3) engineering effort for rollout automation, 4) token accounting surprises from system prompts.
[08:40] Marcus Hale: can Redwood instrument token usage per route in real time?
[08:43] Maya Chen: yes console has token-level breakdown by model/route, and you can export logs for billing reconciliation.
[08:50] Priya Rao: great. any customer references close to our stack?
[08:54] Maya Chen: we have a couple in fintech and retail with similar latency budgets; I can intro you to one customer's CSM for a short chat.
[09:01] Diego Ramos: cool. let's try to get a sample unit-econ with our numbers now if possible?
[09:05] Liam O'Connor: sure, quick back-of-envelope: 600 tokens * hosted rate $0.0014 per 1k tokens = $0.00084 per request. multiply by estimated monthly active requests of 1.2M that's about $1,008/month? wait, math slip—let me recompute. 600 tokens / 1000 = 0.6 * $0.0014 = $0.00084 per request. times 1.2M = $1,008. ok that's below your $35k. but if your active usage grows to 40M requests the delta matters.
[09:39] Priya Rao: that clarifies. our worry is bursty growth; the tail could spike ops cost.
[09:45] Maya Chen: which is exactly where hybrid routing helps—dedicated baseline to absorb steady traffic, hosted for spikes. cost modeling will show the sensitivity.
[09:56] Marcus Hale: what about model choice—are you recommending open models or is Redwood hosting proprietary ones?
[10:02] Liam O'Connor: we support curated open models and some commercial variants; choice depends on your quality and license needs. open models give cost predictability; commercial models sometimes cost more but can improve accuracy.
[10:15] Anya Sato: for the pilot, we'd rather test with the open 33B family if that gives us closer to production quality.
[10:20] Maya Chen: sounds good. we'll prepare a suggested config: open 33B q4 on dedicated baseline + hosted fallback, plus a small eval suite.
[10:30] (fast forward, middle of call, 15-25 minute mark)
[25:10] Liam O'Connor: a couple practical notes: 1) set your batching window to something like 5-10ms to capture small coalescing without big tail, 2) enable prefix caching for session-based prompts, 3) set a quality guardrail with automatic rollback.
[25:30] Marcus Hale: 5-10ms batching window seems fine. any effect on p99?
[25:35] Liam O'Connor: p99 can increase for certain patterns—console can show distribution so you can tune. if p99 matters, consider a low-latency routed pool with smaller batch sizes.
[25:47] Priya Rao: can you give an example of observed savings from prefix cache?
[25:52] Liam O'Connor: one customer saw 36% token reduction on average across chat flows with aggressive prefix reuse.
[26:00] Diego Ramos: what about deployment overhead for model upgrades?
[26:04] Ravi Patel: we support canary rollouts and A/B traffic splits in the Console. you can pin versions per route and automatically roll back on regressions found by Redwood Optimize.
[26:17] Priya Rao: that helps. Diego: anything else from product side?
[26:21] Diego Ramos: just curious about observability retention costs—how much does it cost to keep traces and logs for a year?
[26:28] Maya Chen: that's an add-on; we'll include options in the security/ops sheet.
[26:35] (near end, recap and next steps)
[48:30] Maya Chen: quick recap: Redwood will send a unit econ model, security docs, and a pilot plan. Kaleida will share traffic histograms and confirm beta cohort. we'll reconvene after the initial dataset is shared.
[48:50] Priya Rao: sounds good. Marcus: any blocking concerns?
[48:55] Marcus Hale: mainly proof that we can meet p95 under 250ms and get per-request cost near target.
[49:02] Maya Chen: understood — pilot will cover both.
[49:08] Priya Rao: thanks everyone.
[49:12] Liam O'Connor: thanks all. we'll follow up with dates for pilot kickoff.
[49:20] (call ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional ASR errors (e.g., K-V cache transcribed as 'K-V cash', Redwood Dedicated heard as 'Redwood Dedicate'), speaker attributions approximate.
notes: Customer sharp on latency and budget; receptive to hybrid host/dedicated approach. Pilot agreed as next practical step.
